title: KV access trajectory replay lab notes
body:
Purpose:
Quick notes from repeating and instrumenting offline KV access trajectories to reproduce long-tail bandwidth spikes and eviction cascades we saw in production clusters (2024-11 to 2024-12). Goal is a repeatable lab harness to exercise request interleaving, batching, and spillback behavior with realistic temporal locality.

Summary of approach:
- Collected sampled access traces from prod agent (trace-sampler v0.9) for 3 days on a busy node (node-id: i-prod-07). Each record: key-hash (64b), timestamp, request-id, sequence-length, client-batch-size, model-id. Masked keys for privacy.
- Built a lightweight replayer (kv-replay) that: replays timestamps, supports client fanout, reproduces batching and inter-request jitter, and can replay at scaled time (real-time, 2x, 10x).
- Added per-bank counters via new per-bank-exporter (hw-counters hooked to /proc/kv_bank*) and NVMe read/latency meters.

What we replayed:
- Trace A: 2.1M accesses, predominantly short-chat completions, heavy tail of long contexts; baseline reuse ~0.32.
- Trace B: 420k accesses, 90% embedding requests (high locality within short prefix windows).
- Mixed trace: sampled 10% of A + synthetic hot keys inserted (top-100 hotness) to stress eviction heuristics.

Key commands (lab):
- collect: ./trace-sampler --node i-prod-07 --duration 72h --sample-rate 0.02 --out traceA.pcap
- preprocess: python3 tools/mask_and_aggregate.py --in traceA.pcap --out traceA.masked.json
- replay: ./kv-replay --trace traceA.masked.json --rate-replay real-time --clients 64 --batching-preserve true --pin-bank-policy none
- run with bank counters: sudo ./per-bank-exporter --out bank-metrics.csv & ./kv-replay ...

Observations (first-pass):
1) Reuse collapse when batching increases:
   - Baseline (clients=16, batching-preserve true): observed reuse ~0.31-0.34 (matches prod sample).
   - Increasing clients to 64 while preserving original intra-client batching (more interleaving) dropped reuse to ~0.22.
   - Eviction rate (evict/sec) increased by ~3x in the 64-client scenario; background spillback to NVMe doubled.
   - Interpretation: interleaving churn across clients increases working set diversity seen by each GPU bank and reduces per-key temporal locality, leading to lower residency and more eviction cycles.

2) Bank-skew + microburst amplification:
   - When synthetic hotset was concentrated on a single logical bank (we simulated key->bank mapping to 1 of 8), that bank hit bandwidth saturation quickly (peak read BW ~11.6 GB/s on a 12 GB/s channel reported by exporter).
   - Other banks idled; overall per-node NVMe reads increased because the saturated bank spilled more often rather than balanced eviction across banks.
   - Result: tail-latencies for requests touching the saturated bank spiked 4-8x.

3) Prefetch window misalignment costs:
   - We experimented with prefetch windows of 8KB, 32KB, 128KB worth of entries. Small windows caused thrashing for long-context requests; large windows reduced eviction but increased wasted reads (read amplification on NVMe).
   - Read amplification (extra bytes read / useful bytes) grew from 1.1x (8KB) to ~2.7x (128KB) under mixed workloads. Optimal sweet spot depends on hotset size and observed stride; needs adaptive tuning.

4) Spillback latency and NVMe tail effects:
   - Under sustained microbursts (bursts with >20k reqs/s for 3s windows), NVMe queue depth climbed and average read latency moved from 1.2ms to 6.1ms; p99 went to 18ms.
   - The runtime's async readback backlog produced backpressure which queued more requests, creating a feedback loop that magnified evictions (resident set decreased while I/O latencies increased).

Quantitative snapshot (mixed trace, clients=64, batch-preserve=true):
- Aggregate reuse rate: 0.215
- Evictions/sec: 1780 (vs baseline 560)
- Average NVMe read latency: 2.9ms (baseline 1.1ms)
- NVMe read BW: 420 MB/s -> spikes to 2.8 GB/s during microbursts
- Resident window oscillation period: ~6s (observed cyclic rise/drop in occupancy)

Quick hypotheses / root cause candidates:
- Client-side fanout and request interleaving drives apparent working-set diversity beyond what per-client locality suggests.
- Bank mapping (hash->bank) deterministic skew amplifies hot keys into a single channel causing localized saturation.
- Prefetch heuristics tuned to average-case do not adapt quickly to sudden hotset shifts and therefore either prefetch too little (thrash) or too much (amplify reads).
- Backpressure loops: long NVMe latencies lead to longer service times which increases overlap between requests, increasing instantaneous working set and producing more evictions.

Short term mitigations to test (lab):
- Randomize key->bank mapping per-epoch (epoch = 30s) to amortize hotspots across banks. Measure whether p99 tail reduces without increasing average read amplification.
- Conservative per-bank admission throttling: cap concurrent reads per bank and route overflow to less-loaded banks (requires routing shim).
- Adaptive prefetch window based on observed reuse slope: compute short-window reuse estimate and grow/shrink prefetch.
- Small client-side pacing knobs: reduce client concurrency/batch-stomp by adding jitter to client replay to see impact on reuse.

Longer-term / engineering follow-ups:
- Instrumentation: add per-request residency lifetime histogram, per-bank recent-hotset sampler, and attach those to trace output for future replay correlation. (see PR #812).
- Scheduler: prototype a bank-aware request scheduler that prefers spreading heavy-key requests across channels when possible.
- Eviction policy: evaluate an occupancy-aware variant that biases pinning for keys with high reuse-rate slope.
- Dashboard: add a 'trace-replay' dashboard to console for quick comparison between real-prod traces and replay runs (latency, reuse, evict/sec, nvme BW).

Open action items (todo):
- [ ] Run 10 full replays of Trace A with randomized key->bank mapping; collect p50/p95/p99 and evict/sec. Owner: Kenji. Due: 2025-02-07. (Jira INFR-2345).
- [ ] Add per-request residency histogram to exporter (PR linked). Owner: Lina. Due: 2025-02-14.
- [ ] Validate whether client-side pacing at source reduces reuse collapse in production (pilot with beta customers). Owner: Hassan. Due: 2025-03-01.

Notes to self / rough ideas:
- Could we synthesize a tiny in-process "shadow cache" that tracks local predicted reuse and returns hit hints to the replayer to approximate what full runtime would do w/o touching NVMe? Might speed up experiments.
- We should ensure that replay tool supports tagging synthetic hot keys so tests are deterministic across runs (seed param).
- When running on our small lab rigs, scale traces down but preserve burst shapes (use --preserve-burst flag).

Appendix: quick plot references from run 2025-01-24 (attached locally to lab run directory):
- p99-latency-vs-time.png: shows spikes aligning with bank-1 read bw spike at t=420s.
- reuse-curve.png: sliding-window reuse (30s) showing collapse when client concurrency crosses threshold 32->64.
- bank-occupancy-heatmap.csv: per-bank occupancy over time.

If anyone wants to run these experiments and can't find trace artifacts, see: /mnt/lab-traces/kv-replay/traceA_masked_20250110.tar.gz

End of notes.

-- Maya
